claim: Loss-of-function mutations of KCNJ10 in humans cause seizures and progressive neurological decline.
source: In humans, loss-of-function mutations of KCNJ10, which encodes the inward-rectifying potassium channel KIR4.1, causes seizures and progressive neurological decline.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about human KCNJ10 mutations.

claim: Kir4.1 channels localize to perinodal areas in oligodendrocytes.
source: We observed that Kir4.1 channels localized to perinodal areas and the inner myelin tongue, suggesting roles in juxta-axonal K+ removal.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and immunoelectron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kir4.1 channels localize to the inner myelin tongue.
source: We observed that Kir4.1 channels localized to perinodal areas and the inner myelin tongue, suggesting roles in juxta-axonal K+ removal.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and immunoelectron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conditional knockout of OL-Kcnj10 resulted in late onset mitochondrial damage.
source: Conditional knockout (cKO) of OL-Kcnj10 resulted in late onset mitochondrial damage and axonal degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing increased mitochondrial circularity at P140.

claim: Conditional knockout of OL-Kcnj10 resulted in axonal degeneration.
source: Conditional knockout (cKO) of OL-Kcnj10 resulted in late onset mitochondrial damage and axonal degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry data showing axonal pathology.

claim: Adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice showed delayed visual evoked potentials.
source: This was accompanied by neuronal loss and neuro-axonal dysfunction in adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice as shown by delayed visual evoked potentials, inner retinal thinning and progressive motor deficits.
evidence: This is supported by VEP recordings presented in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice showed inner retinal thinning.
source: This was accompanied by neuronal loss and neuro-axonal dysfunction in adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice as shown by delayed visual evoked potentials, inner retinal thinning and progressive motor deficits.
evidence: This is supported by OCT imaging data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice showed progressive motor deficits.
source: This was accompanied by neuronal loss and neuro-axonal dysfunction in adult OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice as shown by delayed visual evoked potentials, inner retinal thinning and progressive motor deficits.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod performance data in Figure 3C and behavioral videos.

claim: Axon pathologies in OL-Kcnj10 cKO were exacerbated after white matter injury in the spinal cord.
source: Axon pathologies in OL-Kcnj10 cKO were exacerbated after WM injury in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by lysolecithin lesion data presented in Figure 5.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is critical for long-term maintenance of axonal function during adulthood.
source: Our findings point towards a critical role of OL-Kir4.1 for long-term maintenance of axonal function and integrity during adulthood and after WM injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the progressive phenotype observed in adult cKO mice.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is critical for long-term maintenance of axonal integrity after white matter injury.
source: Our findings point towards a critical role of OL-Kir4.1 for long-term maintenance of axonal function and integrity during adulthood and after WM injury.
evidence: This is supported by the lysolecithin lesion experiments showing exacerbated pathology.

claim: Oligodendrocytes maintain metabolic and trophic support of axons by providing lactate in response to sensing of axonal firing.
source: For example, oligodendrocytes (OLs) maintain metabolic and trophic support of axons by providing lactate in response to sensing of axonal firing (Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Saab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Astrocytes are major regulators of neuronal excitability through exchange and buffering of ions such as K+.
source: Exchange and buffering of ions such as K+ between astrocytes (AS) and neurons have been well described and led to the current understanding that those cells are major regulators of neuronal excitability (Cui et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2014; Kelley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kir4.1 is a highly conserved ATP- and pH-sensitive K+ channel expressed in both astrocytes and oligodendrocyte cells of the CNS.
source: Here, we focused on Kir4.1 (Kcnj10), a highly conserved ATP- and pH-sensitive K+ channel expressed in both AS and OL cells of the CNS (Hibino et al., 2004; Tanemoto et al., 2000; Hibino et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kir channels regulate K+ transmembrane gradients.
source: Kir channels regulate K+ transmembrane gradients (Rash, 2010; Menichella et al., 2006; Olsen and Sontheimer, 2008; Chever et al., 2010), which are critical for action potential propagation as well as axonal K+ outflow that is necessary to establish resting membrane potential and neuronal repolarization (Yasuda et al., 2008; Seifert et al., 2009; Djukic et al., 2007; Bay and Butt, 2012; Sibille et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: K+ transmembrane gradients are critical for action potential propagation.
source: Kir channels regulate K+ transmembrane gradients (Rash, 2010; Menichella et al., 2006; Olsen and Sontheimer, 2008; Chever et al., 2010), which are critical for action potential propagation as well as axonal K+ outflow that is necessary to establish resting membrane potential and neuronal repolarization (Yasuda et al., 2008; Seifert et al., 2009; Djukic et al., 2007; Bay and Butt, 2012; Sibille et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Axonal K+ outflow is necessary to establish resting membrane potential and neuronal repolarization.
source: Kir channels regulate K+ transmembrane gradients (Rash, 2010; Menichella et al., 2006; Olsen and Sontheimer, 2008; Chever et al., 2010), which are critical for action potential propagation as well as axonal K+ outflow that is necessary to establish resting membrane potential and neuronal repolarization (Yasuda et al., 2008; Seifert et al., 2009; Djukic et al., 2007; Bay and Butt, 2012; Sibille et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kir4.1 can form homo- and heterotetrameric associations with Kir5.1.
source: Its complex expression pattern, including homo- and heterotetrameric association with Kir5.1 (Kcnj16), underlies potentially diverse roles depending on glial cell sub-type and CNS anatomical regions (Cui et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2014; Kelley et al., 2018; Hibino et al., 2004; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homotetrameric Kir4.1 is the major inward-rectifying K+ channel in oligodendrocytes.
source: Homotetrameric Kir4.1 is the major inward-rectifying K+ channel in OLs, and its downregulation has been reported in glial cells in CNS disease (Zurolo et al., 2012; Eberhardt et al., 2011; Schirmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Downregulation of Kir4.1 has been reported in glial cells in CNS disease.
source: Homotetrameric Kir4.1 is the major inward-rectifying K+ channel in OLs, and its downregulation has been reported in glial cells in CNS disease (Zurolo et al., 2012; Eberhardt et al., 2011; Schirmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Glial Kir4.1 channels help remove extracellular K+ during neuronal activity.
source: Because glial Kir4.1 channels help remove extracellular K+ during neuronal activity, general loss-of-function is associated with severe human neurological conditions.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of Kir4.1 function.

claim: Human congenital KCNJ10 loss-of-function mutations in EAST/SeSAME syndrome cause electrolyte imbalance, seizures, pathological changes in the retina, sensorineural deafness and progressive motor deficits.
source: Human congenital KCNJ10 loss-of-function mutations in EAST/SeSAME syndrome cause electrolyte imbalance, seizures, pathological changes in the retina, sensorineural deafness and progressive motor deficits in affected individuals (Bockenhauer et al., 2009; Cross et al., 2013; Scholl et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical literature.

claim: Mice lacking glial-Kcnj10 show early lethality in young adulthood, attributable to increased neuronal excitability and epileptic activity.
source: Prior reports have found early lethality in young adult mice lacking glial-Kcnj10, attributable to increased neuronal excitability and epileptic activity (Djukic et al., 2007; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Conditional ablation of Kcnj10 using Gfap-cre was lethal before P30.
source: In particular, conditional ablation of Kcnj10 using Gfap-cre (that targets both AS and OL glial cell types) was lethal before P30 (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2001), an early/severe phenotype that precluded study of late functions in adult white matter (WM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The number of ON OL-Kir4.1+ channels increased with age in control littermates.
source: While in control littermates the number of ON OL-Kir4.1+ channels increased with age (Figure 1A–C), we observed significantly lower Kir4.1 and Kir5.1 protein levels in Kcnj10 cKO mice expressing cre recombinase under control of the Olig2 promoter (Figure 1A–B; note that persistent expression corresponds to intact AS Kir4.1 in cKO animals) (Schüller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Significantly lower Kir4.1 and Kir5.1 protein levels were observed in Kcnj10 cKO mice expressing cre recombinase under control of the Olig2 promoter.
source: While in control littermates the number of ON OL-Kir4.1+ channels increased with age (Figure 1A–C), we observed significantly lower Kir4.1 and Kir5.1 protein levels in Kcnj10 cKO mice expressing cre recombinase under control of the Olig2 promoter (Figure 1A–B; note that persistent expression corresponds to intact AS Kir4.1 in cKO animals) (Schüller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Kir4.1 staining was substantially reduced from Apc+ OL cell bodies in ON samples from adult Olig2-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl mice.
source: As shown (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Kir4.1 staining was substantially reduced from Apc+ OL cell bodies but not Gfap+ astrocyte fibers in ON samples from adult Olig2-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-1) and Cnp-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-2) mice (Figure 1D) confirming robust knockout efficiency in OLs (Djukic et al., 2007; Schüller et al., 2008; Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kir4.1 staining was substantially reduced from Apc+ OL cell bodies in ON samples from adult Cnp-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl mice.
source: As shown (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Kir4.1 staining was substantially reduced from Apc+ OL cell bodies but not Gfap+ astrocyte fibers in ON samples from adult Olig2-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-1) and Cnp-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-2) mice (Figure 1D) confirming robust knockout efficiency in OLs (Djukic et al., 2007; Schüller et al., 2008; Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kir4.1 staining was not substantially reduced from Gfap+ astrocyte fibers in ON samples from adult Olig2-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl and Cnp-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl mice.
source: As shown (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Kir4.1 staining was substantially reduced from Apc+ OL cell bodies but not Gfap+ astrocyte fibers in ON samples from adult Olig2-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-1) and Cnp-cre:Kir4.1fl/fl (cKO-2) mice (Figure 1D) confirming robust knockout efficiency in OLs (Djukic et al., 2007; Schüller et al., 2008; Lappe-Siefke et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1D.

claim: Levels of Kcnj10 transcripts were higher in myelinating OLs compared to OPCs in vitro.
source: Levels of Kcnj10 transcripts were higher in myelinating OLs compared to OPCs in vitro, whereas Kcnj16 mRNA decreased during OL maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) (Kalsi et al., 2004; Nwaobi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kcnj16 mRNA decreased during OL maturation in vitro.
source: Levels of Kcnj10 transcripts were higher in myelinating OLs compared to OPCs in vitro, whereas Kcnj16 mRNA decreased during OL maturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) (Kalsi et al., 2004; Nwaobi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Higher Cacna1c mRNA levels were observed in the setting of loss-of-OPC-encoded Kcnj10 in-vitro.
source: Notably, we observed higher Cacna1c mRNA levels in the setting of loss-of-OPC-encoded Kcnj10 in-vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (Paez et al., 2010; Cheli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cacna1c encodes Cav1.2, a major voltage-gated Ca2+ channel in OPCs.
source: Cacna1c encodes Cav1.2, a major voltage-gated Ca2+ channel in OPCs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Kir4.1 immunogold particles were abundant in white matter astrocyte fibers.
source: In WM AS, Kir4.1 immunogold particles were abundant in fibers and particular seen in processes in contact to the outer myelin tongue, in perivascular end feet and adjacent to the node of Ranvier (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Kir4.1 immunogold particles were particularly seen in astrocyte processes in contact to the outer myelin tongue.
source: In WM AS, Kir4.1 immunogold particles were abundant in fibers and particular seen in processes in contact to the outer myelin tongue, in perivascular end feet and adjacent to the node of Ranvier (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Kir4.1 immunogold particles were particularly seen in astrocyte perivascular end feet.
source: In WM AS, Kir4.1 immunogold particles were abundant in fibers and particular seen in processes in contact to the outer myelin tongue, in perivascular end feet and adjacent to the node of Ranvier (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Kir4.1 immunogold particles were particularly seen in astrocyte processes adjacent to the node of Ranvier.
source: In WM AS, Kir4.1 immunogold particles were abundant in fibers and particular seen in processes in contact to the outer myelin tongue, in perivascular end feet and adjacent to the node of Ranvier (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data in Figure 1F-G.

claim: OPCs lacking Kcnj10 exhibited precocious cell cycle exits.
source: We found that OPCs lacking Kcnj10 exhibited precocious cell cycle exits as shown by decreased numbers of dividing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B) and earlier onset of myelin production (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU and EdU incorporation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: OPCs lacking Kcnj10 showed earlier onset of myelin production.
source: We found that OPCs lacking Kcnj10 exhibited precocious cell cycle exits as shown by decreased numbers of dividing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B) and earlier onset of myelin production (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Mbp immunostaining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Decreased mRNA levels of Uhrf1 were found in OPCs lacking Kcnj10.
source: In addition, we found decreased mRNA levels of cell cycle and progenitor cell markers, such as Uhrf1 and Nkx2-2 in OPCs and conversely observed increased myelin basic protein (Mbp) mRNA levels in OLs in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F) (Magri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Decreased mRNA levels of Nkx2-2 were found in OPCs lacking Kcnj10.
source: In addition, we found decreased mRNA levels of cell cycle and progenitor cell markers, such as Uhrf1 and Nkx2-2 in OPCs and conversely observed increased myelin basic protein (Mbp) mRNA levels in OLs in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F) (Magri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Increased myelin basic protein (Mbp) mRNA levels were observed in OLs lacking Kcnj10 in vitro.
source: In addition, we found decreased mRNA levels of cell cycle and progenitor cell markers, such as Uhrf1 and Nkx2-2 in OPCs and conversely observed increased myelin basic protein (Mbp) mRNA levels in OLs in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F) (Magri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Mice deficient in OL-encoded Kcnj10 had normal g-ratios in ON tissue at P40.
source: Mice deficient in OL-encoded Kcnj10 had normal g-ratios in ON tissue at P40 (Figure 2A–B); however, they showed slightly smaller g-ratios in spinal WM tracts corresponding to thicker myelin sheaths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Mice deficient in OL-encoded Kcnj10 showed slightly smaller g-ratios in spinal WM tracts at P40 corresponding to thicker myelin sheaths.
source: Mice deficient in OL-encoded Kcnj10 had normal g-ratios in ON tissue at P40 (Figure 2A–B); however, they showed slightly smaller g-ratios in spinal WM tracts corresponding to thicker myelin sheaths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Axonal diameters were not different in ON samples between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: Axonal diameters were not different in both ON and spinal WM samples at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2C.

claim: Axonal diameters were not different in spinal WM samples between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: Axonal diameters were not different in both ON and spinal WM samples at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity was not different in the ON between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity and density of mitochondria was not different in the ON and spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The density of mitochondria was not different in the ON between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity and density of mitochondria was not different in the ON and spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2C.

claim: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity was not different in the spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity and density of mitochondria was not different in the ON and spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D.

claim: The density of mitochondria was not different in the spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: The morphology of intra-axonal mitochondria with respect to circularity and density of mitochondria was not different in the ON and spinal cord WM between control and Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The density of mature Apc+ Olig2+ OLs was transiently higher in Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40.
source: Notably, the density of mature Apc+ Olig2+ OLs was transiently higher in Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40, however, normalized during adulthood (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The density of mature Apc+ Olig2+ OLs normalized during adulthood in Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: Notably, the density of mature Apc+ Olig2+ OLs was transiently higher in Kcnj10 cKO mice at P40, however, normalized during adulthood (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2D-E.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is involved in regulating cell cycle exit during early postnatal development.
source: These results suggest that OL-Kir4.1 is involved in regulating cell cycle exit and OL differentiation during early postnatal development but is not a requirement for normal myelination.
evidence: This is inferred from the precocious differentiation phenotype observed.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is involved in regulating OL differentiation during early postnatal development.
source: These results suggest that OL-Kir4.1 is involved in regulating cell cycle exit and OL differentiation during early postnatal development but is not a requirement for normal myelination.
evidence: This is inferred from the precocious differentiation phenotype observed.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is not a requirement for normal myelination.
source: These results suggest that OL-Kir4.1 is involved in regulating cell cycle exit and OL differentiation during early postnatal development but is not a requirement for normal myelination.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal g-ratios observed at P40.

claim: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited progressive neurological symptoms including abnormal gait and ataxia starting as early as three months of age.
source: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited progressive neurological symptoms including abnormal gait and ataxia (Video 1), generalized seizures (Video 2) and hindlimb clasping (Videos 3 and 4) starting as early as three months of age.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and videos.

claim: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited generalized seizures starting as early as three months of age.
source: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited progressive neurological symptoms including abnormal gait and ataxia (Video 1), generalized seizures (Video 2) and hindlimb clasping (Videos 3 and 4) starting as early as three months of age.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and videos.

claim: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited hindlimb clasping starting as early as three months of age.
source: Both Kcnj10-cKO lines exhibited progressive neurological symptoms including abnormal gait and ataxia (Video 1), generalized seizures (Video 2) and hindlimb clasping (Videos 3 and 4) starting as early as three months of age.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and videos.

claim: Early lethality by 6 months of age was observed in ~70% of Cnp-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: Early lethality by 6 months of age, most likely due to complications of epileptic seizures, was observed in ~70% of Cnp-cre and ~40% in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO mice (Figure 3A) (Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 3A.

claim: Early lethality by 6 months of age was observed in ~40% of Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: Early lethality by 6 months of age, most likely due to complications of epileptic seizures, was observed in ~70% of Cnp-cre and ~40% in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO mice (Figure 3A) (Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 3A.

claim: Early lethality in Kcnj10 cKO mice was most likely due to complications of epileptic seizures.
source: Early lethality by 6 months of age, most likely due to complications of epileptic seizures, was observed in ~70% of Cnp-cre and ~40% in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO mice (Figure 3A) (Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of seizures and prior literature.

claim: Higher seizure frequencies were a common feature of both cKO lines with increasing age.
source: Higher seizure frequencies were a common feature of both cKO lines with increasing age, in keeping with prior findings (Djukic et al., 2007; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and citations to prior literature.

claim: All cKO mice showed reduced body weights versus control littermates at P140.
source: All cKO mice showed reduced body weights versus control littermates at P140 (Figure 3B), and we found motor dysfunction as shown by reduced rotarod performance in both cKO cohorts at P140 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements in Figure 3B.

claim: Motor dysfunction was shown by reduced rotarod performance in both cKO cohorts at P140.
source: All cKO mice showed reduced body weights versus control littermates at P140 (Figure 3B), and we found motor dysfunction as shown by reduced rotarod performance in both cKO cohorts at P140 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by rotarod performance data in Figure 3C.

claim: Both Kcnj10 cKO lines had delayed VEP latencies at P140.
source: Here, both Kcnj10 cKO lines had delayed VEP latencies at P140 (Figure 3D–E) indicating dysfunction in the visual system.
evidence: This is supported by VEP recording data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Delayed VEP latencies indicate dysfunction in the visual system.
source: Here, both Kcnj10 cKO lines had delayed VEP latencies at P140 (Figure 3D–E) indicating dysfunction in the visual system.
evidence: This is inferred from the VEP data.

claim: OCT imaging showed thinning of inner retinal layers in cKO mice at P140.
source: In addition, we studied structural changes in the retina of live animals utilizing optical coherence tomography (OCT), where the thickness of specific retinal layers can be used as a surrogate for retinal ganglion cell (RGC) survival. Indeed, OCT imaging showed thinning of inner retinal layers (IRL) in cKO mice at P140 revealing a reduction in the number of ganglion cells and their corresponding axons (Figure 3F) (Cruz-Herranz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by OCT imaging data in Figure 3F.

claim: Thinning of inner retinal layers reveals a reduction in the number of ganglion cells and their corresponding axons.
source: In addition, we studied structural changes in the retina of live animals utilizing optical coherence tomography (OCT), where the thickness of specific retinal layers can be used as a surrogate for retinal ganglion cell (RGC) survival. Indeed, OCT imaging showed thinning of inner retinal layers (IRL) in cKO mice at P140 revealing a reduction in the number of ganglion cells and their corresponding axons (Figure 3F) (Cruz-Herranz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the OCT data and cited literature.

claim: Permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in visual dysfunction with retinal atrophy in adult mice.
source: In summary, permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in visual dysfunction with retinal atrophy in adult mice as well as motor deficits and early mortality.
evidence: This is supported by VEP, OCT, and RGC count data.

claim: Permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in motor deficits in adult mice.
source: In summary, permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in visual dysfunction with retinal atrophy in adult mice as well as motor deficits and early mortality.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod and behavioral data.

claim: Permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in early mortality in adult mice.
source: In summary, permanent loss-of-Kcnj10 function in OLs results in visual dysfunction with retinal atrophy in adult mice as well as motor deficits and early mortality.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 3A.

claim: Decreased Mbp protein levels were observed in ON lysates from 6 month old Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: We observed decreased Mbp protein levels, a critical myelin component, in ON and spinal cord lysates from 6 month old Kcnj10 cKO mice, which could explain the delayed VEP latencies observed in older animals (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A.

claim: Decreased Mbp protein levels were observed in spinal cord lysates from 6 month old Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: We observed decreased Mbp protein levels, a critical myelin component, in ON and spinal cord lysates from 6 month old Kcnj10 cKO mice, which could explain the delayed VEP latencies observed in older animals (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Decreased Mbp protein levels could explain the delayed VEP latencies observed in older animals.
source: We observed decreased Mbp protein levels, a critical myelin component, in ON and spinal cord lysates from 6 month old Kcnj10 cKO mice, which could explain the delayed VEP latencies observed in older animals (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is speculated based on the correlation between Mbp loss and VEP delays.

claim: A substantial loss of Kir4.1 protein could be detected in Kcnj10 cKO ON tissue at P180.
source: A substantial loss of Kir4.1 protein could be detected in Kcnj10 cKO ON and spinal cord tissue at P180 confirming robust knockout efficiency at that age (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A substantial loss of Kir4.1 protein could be detected in Kcnj10 cKO spinal cord tissue at P180.
source: A substantial loss of Kir4.1 protein could be detected in Kcnj10 cKO ON and spinal cord tissue at P180 confirming robust knockout efficiency at that age (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Disorganization of WM tracts was observed at ultrastructural level in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO ON at P140.
source: Additionally, at ultrastructural level, we observed disorganization of WM tracts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and loss of myelin compactness in a subset of axons as well as evidence for axonal degeneration in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO ON and spinal cord tissue at P140 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of myelin compactness in a subset of axons was observed in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO ON at P140.
source: Additionally, at ultrastructural level, we observed disorganization of WM tracts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and loss of myelin compactness in a subset of axons as well as evidence for axonal degeneration in Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO ON and spinal cord tissue at P140 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 4B.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 plays a major role in long-term neuro-axonal maintenance and integrity of long WM tracts of the ON and spinal cord.

evidence: This is inferred from the cumulative data showing progressive pathology in cKO mice.

evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 14 days post-lysolecithin-induced focal demyelination, mitochondria in axons from Olig2-cre driven Kcnj10 cKO animals were significantly more swollen/circular than their control counterparts.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 is dispensable for (re)myelination.
source: These results indicate that OL-Kir4.1 is dispensable for (re)myelination but that its function is crucial for axon support and maintenance after long-term demyelinating WM injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal g-ratios observed in both acute and chronic lesions.

claim: OL-Kir4.1 function is crucial for axon support and maintenance after long-term demyelinating WM injury.
source: These results indicate that OL-Kir4.1 is dispensable for (re)myelination but that its function is crucial for axon support and maintenance after long-term demyelinating WM injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the mitochondrial and axonal pathologies observed at 60 dpl.

claim: The lactate transporter MCT1 shows a similar juxta-axonal expression pattern to Kir4.1.
source: Because the lactate transporter MCT1 also shows a similar juxta-axonal expression pattern (Lee et al., 2012), it is possible that other ion channels and solute carrier transporters are arrayed in a similar way to maintain axon energy, activity and integrity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It is possible that other ion channels and solute carrier transporters are arrayed in a similar way to maintain axon energy, activity and integrity.

claim: Kir4.1 comprises a 'myelin nanochannel'.
source: Thus, we propose that Kir4.1 comprises a 'myelin nanochannel'.
evidence: This is proposed based on the localization of Kir4.1 at the inner myelin tongue.

claim: The positioning of Kir4.1 is consistent with a role in siphoning K+ within myelin segments.
source: While this positioning is consistent with a role in siphoning K+ within myelin segments, further studies are needed to confirm this function.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data.

source: Regarding early developmental requirements of OL-Kir4.1 function, the cKO resulted in somewhat precocious maturation and myelination.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing earlier cell cycle exit and myelin production.

claim: Precocious maturation suggests either a direct role in regulating differentiation or indirect effects of altered ion currents on voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in Kcnj10-deficient OPCs.
source: This suggests either a direct role in regulating differentiation or indirect effects of altered ion currents on voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in Kcnj10-deficient OPCs (Paez et al., 2010; Cheli et al., 2015; Cheli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculated based on the precocious maturation phenotype and cited literature.

claim: Based on observations during development and regeneration, Kir4.1 regulates, but is not required for normal myelination.
source: Based on observations during development and regeneration, we conclude that Kir4.1 regulates, but is not required for normal myelination.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal g-ratios observed despite precocious maturation.

claim: Other studies have indicated early roles for OL-Kir4.1 channels in support of acute axonal activity.
source: Other studies have indicated early roles for OL-Kir4.1 channels in support of acute axonal activity (Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of OL-Kir4.1 currents can in principle be compensated for by OPC- or AS-encoded Kir4.1/Kir5.1 channels, or homotetrameric Kir5.1 channels with PSD-95.
source: While in principle, loss of OL-Kir4.1 currents can be compensated for by OPC- or AS-encoded Kir4.1/Kir5.1 channels, or homotetrameric Kir5.1 channels with PSD-95 (Hibino et al., 2010; Tanemoto et al., 2002), it is evident that such compensation eventually fails during adulthood in OL-specific Kcnj10 cKO mice, possibly due to increasing demand for perinodal K+ buffering during sustained electric activity, such as with physical exertion (rotarod performance) or after (excitotoxic) demyelinating WM injury.
evidence: This is speculated based on the progressive phenotype and cited literature.

claim: Compensation for loss of OL-Kir4.1 currents eventually fails during adulthood in OL-specific Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: While in principle, loss of OL-Kir4.1 currents can be compensated for by OPC- or AS-encoded Kir4.1/Kir5.1 channels, or homotetrameric Kir5.1 channels with PSD-95 (Hibino et al., 2010; Tanemoto et al., 2002), it is evident that such compensation eventually fails during adulthood in OL-specific Kcnj10 cKO mice, possibly due to increasing demand for perinodal K+ buffering during sustained electric activity, such as with physical exertion (rotarod performance) or after (excitotoxic) demyelinating WM injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the progressive phenotype observed in adult cKO mice.

claim: Failure of compensation is possibly due to increasing demand for perinodal K+ buffering during sustained electric activity.
source: While in principle, loss of OL-Kir4.1 currents can be compensated for by OPC- or AS-encoded Kir4.1/Kir5.1 channels, or homotetrameric Kir5.1 channels with PSD-95 (Hibino et al., 2010; Tanemoto et al., 2002), it is evident that such compensation eventually fails during adulthood in OL-specific Kcnj10 cKO mice, possibly due to increasing demand for perinodal K+ buffering during sustained electric activity, such as with physical exertion (rotarod performance) or after (excitotoxic) demyelinating WM injury.
evidence: This is speculated based on the progressive phenotype.

claim: Kcnj10 expression increases in OLs during maturation and aging.
source: Indeed, we found that Kir4.1 (Kcnj10) expression increases in OLs during maturation and aging, and consistent with progressive requirements in adults, it has been reported that Kir4.1-mediated K+ buffering becomes more important during ON high-frequency stimulation and that OL-Kcnj10 loss-of-function increases neuronal excitability in adult mice (Bay and Butt, 2012; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the data showing age-dependent upregulation of Kir4.1.

claim: Kir4.1-mediated K+ buffering becomes more important during ON high-frequency stimulation.
source: Indeed, we found that Kir4.1 (Kcnj10) expression increases in OLs during maturation and aging, and consistent with progressive requirements in adults, it has been reported that Kir4.1-mediated K+ buffering becomes more important during ON high-frequency stimulation and that OL-Kcnj10 loss-of-function increases neuronal excitability in adult mice (Bay and Butt, 2012; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: OL-Kcnj10 loss-of-function increases neuronal excitability in adult mice.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice without AS-encoded Kcnj10 lack spinal WM tract abnormalities typical of OL-encoded Kir4.1 cKO mice.

evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data comparing AS-specific and OL-specific cKO mice.

claim: The data parses out the specific roles of OL-Kir4.1 and reveals a new supportive role of OLs for long-term axonal maintenance.
source: Thus, our data parses out the specific roles of OL-Kir4.1 and reveals a new supportive role of OLs for long-term axonal maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between OL-specific and AS-specific cKO mice.

claim: Developmental upregulation of OL-Kir4.1 is linked to increasing needs for axonal K+ homeostasis during adulthood.
source: Overall, our findings suggest a model in which developmental upregulation of OL-Kir4.1 is linked to increasing needs for axonal K+ homeostasis during adulthood.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the cumulative findings.

claim: Siphoning of K+ is most likely established through an orchestrated action of juxta-axonal and perinodal glial Kir4.1 channels.
source: Siphoning of K+ is most likely established through an orchestrated action of juxta-axonal and perinodal glial Kir4.1 channels.
evidence: This is speculated based on the localization data.

claim: The ad-axonal expression pattern of mature OL-Kir4.1 channels emphasizes that those channels might have an essential role in K+ clearance from axons.
source: The ad-axonal expression pattern of mature OL-Kir4.1 channels emphasizes that those channels might have an essential role in K+ clearance from axons, a function that becomes more critical later in life.
evidence: This is speculated based on the localization and age-dependent phenotype.

claim: K+ clearance from axons becomes more critical later in life.
source: The ad-axonal expression pattern of mature OL-Kir4.1 channels emphasizes that those channels might have an essential role in K+ clearance from axons, a function that becomes more critical later in life.
evidence: This is inferred from the progressive phenotype observed in adult cKO mice.

claim: Motor dysfunction and spastic paraplegia are progressive age-related neurological symptoms in individuals with EAST/SeSAME syndrome.
source: Indeed, motor dysfunction and spastic paraplegia are progressive age-related neurological symptoms in individuals with EAST/SeSAME syndrome (Cross et al., 2013), which would resemble features that come with permanent knockout of mature OL-Kir4.1 channels resulting in mitochondrial damage and progressive neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior clinical literature.

claim: Features of EAST/SeSAME syndrome resemble features that come with permanent knockout of mature OL-Kir4.1 channels resulting in mitochondrial damage and progressive neurodegeneration.

evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between human and mouse phenotypes.

claim: Increased numbers and swelling of mitochondria as well as enlarged axon diameters were early indicators of impending axonal degeneration in OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice.
source: Increased numbers and swelling of mitochondria as well as enlarged axon diameters were early indicators of impending axonal degeneration in OL-Kcnj10 cKO mice, especially when challenged with focal WM demyelination.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal progression of pathology observed.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Morphological changes of intra-axonal mitochondria have been associated with axonal degeneration in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).

claim: In EAE, mitochondrial changes might characterize a phenomenon that is reversible and precede ultimate axonal degeneration.

claim: Higher seizure frequencies with increasing age might contribute to chronic cognitive and motivational dysfunction in cKO animals.
source: Notably, higher seizure frequencies with increasing age might contribute to chronic cognitive and motivational dysfunction in cKO animals; however, it is unlikely that this has a major effect on degenerative changes in long white matter tracts.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed seizures.

claim: It is unlikely that higher seizure frequencies have a major effect on degenerative changes in long white matter tracts.
source: Notably, higher seizure frequencies with increasing age might contribute to chronic cognitive and motivational dysfunction in cKO animals; however, it is unlikely that this has a major effect on degenerative changes in long white matter tracts.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the data.

claim: OL-encoded Kcnj10 has a novel role in long-term maintenance of axons in WM tracts of the CNS.
source: In summary, we identified that OL-Kir4.1 channels are localized to myelin inner tongue and juxta-nodal regions suggesting functions in removal of K+ commensurate with axonal activity. Moreover, we describe a novel role for OL-encoded Kcnj10 in long-term maintenance of axons in WM tracts of the CNS.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the cumulative data.

claim: Permanent loss of OL-Kir4.1 channels resulted in progressive damage to axons and ultimately loss of neurons with increasing age.
source: Permanent loss of OL-Kir4.1 channels resulted in progressive damage to axons and ultimately loss of neurons with increasing age.
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative pathology data.

claim: The findings raise the question of whether similar mechanisms might exist in Schwann cells that serve the myelinating function in the peripheral nervous system.
source: Our findings raise the question of whether similar mechanisms might exist in Schwann cells that serve the myelinating function in the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This is a question raised based on the findings.

claim: The findings might have relevance for understanding mechanisms of axonal degeneration in chronic MS lesions, where KIR4.1 channels are dysregulated and lost during lesion progression.
source: Additionally, our finding might have relevance for understanding mechanisms of axonal degeneration in chronic MS lesions, where KIR4.1 channels are dysregulated and lost during lesion progression (Schirmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Dissecting mechanisms of dysregulated K+ homeostasis in chronic neuro-inflammatory conditions could help develop neuroprotective strategies designed to correct local peri-axonal K+ imbalances.
source: If so, dissecting mechanisms of dysregulated K+ homeostasis in chronic neuro-inflammatory conditions could help develop neuroprotective strategies designed to correct local peri-axonal K+ imbalances.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential therapeutic implication.
